paper_title: HairDeck: Animation-Ready Stylized Hair Cards from a Single Image

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The hair of stylized characters in games and avatars is built from hair cards: artist-placed ribbons whose geometry is the visible hair, animated by spring bones. Existing image-based methods produce realistic hair or a single fused mesh, while CHARM, the only generator of stylized hair cards, decodes a hairstyle autoregressively as a long sequence of control points. Observing that a card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, we propose HairDeck, which generates it as one: each card is a single token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all cards together. From a single image, HairDeck generates the cards and the spring-bone chains that drive them, yielding an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats. On CHARM's own test set, it lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster, and from single images it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand-based methods. Project page: https://hyzcluster.github.io/HairDeck

sections.content: The hair of stylized characters in games and avatars is built from hair cards: artist-placed ribbons whose geometry is the visible hair, animated by spring bones. Existing imagebased methods produce realistic hair or single fused mesh, while CHARM, the only generator of stylized hair cards, decodes hairstyle autoregressively as long sequence of control points. Observing that card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, we propose HairDeck, which generates it as one: each card is single token, and set diffusion transformer denoises all cards together. From single image, HairDeck generates the cards and the spring-bone chains that drive them, yielding an animatable *Equal contribution. Corresponding authors. asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats. On CHARMs own test set, it lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster, and from single images it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand-based methods. Project page: https://hyzcluster.github.io/ HairDeck 1. Introduction 3D generators now produce convincing shapes from single image [71, 72, 77, 83], but not the structure that artists build assets from. The hair of stylized characters in games It is made of hair cards: and avatars is clear example. few dozen to over hundred ribbons, each placed by an artist, whose geometry is the visible hair. Unlike the alphatextured hair cards of realistic hair, flat strips whose texture stands in for many strands [20, 60, 88], these cards have rhombic or triangular cross-section whose width and thickness vary along the card. Such hair is commonly animated with spring bones: short chains of bones hung from the head whose tips are simulated every frame, so that the hair sways and settles. Similar simulations ship as Dynamic Bone in Unity [18], PhysBones in VRChat [61], Kawaii Physics in Unreal Engine [36] and node in Godot [10]. Artists place every card and rig every chain by hand. Existing methods do not produce this asset. Hair generators output realistic strands [13, 42, 49], including recent ones that accept stylized images [28, 32, 44, 65], and card extraction turns such strands into alpha-textured cards for realistic hair [60, 88]. Image-to-3D generators [72, 77] output single fused mesh with no cards to animate. CHARM [15] is the only generator of stylized hair cards It generates the and introduced the benchmark for them. control points of hairstyle one at time, as sequence of hundreds to thousands of discretized tokens. We observe that card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, and we generate it as one. Like CHARM, we describe each card by its control points (position, width and thickness), and we add its cross-section type and its root normal, the width direction at the root, so each card keeps the cross-section and the orientation the artist gave it. What we change is the unit of generation, with two designs. First, each card becomes one continuous token: card VAE encodes its variable-length control points into latent, and the token holds this latent with the cards root position, root normal and cross-section type, so hairstyle has one token per card, about 70 on average. Second, all tokens of hairstyle are generated together: set diffusion transformer without positional embedding denoises them with flow matching [25, 27], and an existence flag on each token decides how many cards appear. Each design makes generation more accurate and faster. Together they amount to simple rule for assets made of artist-defined primitives: one token per primitive, and no order among them. single image shows the hair relative to the head, so we predict the cards in head frame anchored to the face, which improves where the hair sits without changing its shape. Images also come in many drawing styles, so we widen the appearance of our training renders in two ways: synthetic style augmentation, which improves accuracy on stylized inputs, and renders restyled by an image-editing model [68], which keep the card structure stable across styles. Cards alone do not move. We generate the spring-bone chains with the same recipe: each chain becomes one token holding its path, joint count and stiffness, and second set diffusion transformer generates all chains of hairstyle together from its card tokens. With fixed geometric skinning, the cards and chains form an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats. In summary, our contributions are: card token for stylized hair: representation that keeps the cross-section type and the root normal, and card VAE that encodes the variable-length control points into one continuous latent and decodes the card by arc length. set formulation of hair-card generation: set diffusion transformer without positional embedding generates all card tokens of hairstyle together, and an existence flag on each token decides how many cards appear. Single-image generation with face-anchored head frame, synthetic style augmentation and restyled renders. Spring-bone chains generated as second set conditioned on the card tokens, which makes the output animatable. We evaluate on CHARMs test set with its protocol and also measure the orientation of every card against the original artist meshes. HairDeck lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster. From single image, it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand generators. 2. Related Work Strand-based hair modeling. Hair reconstruction methods can recover strands from multi-view images or videos [31, 35, 41, 48, 57, 70, 80] and from single images [50, 69, 86, 87]. Generative models synthesize strands from latent codes [13, 90], text [49] and images [42]. Recent ones accept stylized or anime images [28, 32, 44, 65], but their output is still strands, the representation of realistic hair. The stylized hair we generate uses cards instead. Hair cards. Real-time engines render realistic hair with textured strips [20], the alpha-textured hair cards whose texture stands in for many strands. Zheng et al. [88] and Strands2Cards [60] convert strand grooms into such cards, HairLRM [44] applies the former to its generated strands, CGHair [33] reconstructs card-based hair from multi-view images, Lee et al. [22] inpaint strips from the sparse strands of single portrait with diffusion model on the scalp UV map, HairCS [30] turns cards back into strands, and production tools ship card generators for grooms [8, 46]. Stylized hair uses different card, whose geometry is the visible hair. CHARM [15] introduced the generation of such cards with control-point representation, dataset of anime hairstyles (the benchmark we use) and an autoregressive transformer that emits the control points of hairstyle one at time. We add the cross-section type and the root normal to its description of card and change the unit of generation. Stylized 3D characters. Image-based methods for anime characters reconstruct stylized heads [5] or full characters [38, 64], and others separate the body, clothing and 2 Figure 2. Overview. Left: hairstyle is set of hair cards. Each card, polyline of control points with width and thickness, becomes one token holding its root position, root normal, card VAE latent z, cross-section type and existence flag. Middle: the set DiT denoises the token set with flow matching, attending across cards and to the condition, point cloud or an image. Empty slots let the model decide how many cards to generate. Right: the card VAE decodes the tokens into cards, and the chain DiT generates their spring-bone chains. hair into components [14, 16, 40]. In all of them the hair is continuous surface, fused with the character or as separate component, rather than set of cards. Earlier work modeled anime and cartoon hair from sketches, skeletons or parametric clumps [34, 43, 76] or as 2.5D layers [79]. Structured and set generation. Native 3D generators encode shapes as latent sets [4, 81, 83, 85] or structured latents [71, 72] and output single surface. Assets built from discrete elements are mostly generated autoregressively: meshes as sequences of face or vertex tokens [6, 12, 45, 66, 84], ordered along triangle strips and UV charts in Strips as Tokens [73], and shapes as sequences of primitives [78]. Other work generates the elements of an asset together. 3DTopia-XL [7] gives each primitive one token and denoises the tokens with diffusion transformer without positional encoding. StrokeFusion [89] encodes each sketch stroke with VAE and diffuses the unordered set of stroke latents with presence flags. DiffuScene [59], SALAD [21], MeshFlow [56], BrepGen [74] and PartCrafter [24] jointly generate the objects of scene, part latents, the triangles of mesh, the faces of CAD models and the parts of objects. We build on this set formulation and design it for hair cards: card VAE turns each card into one token, the set is conditioned on point cloud or single image, and second set of spring-bone chains is conditioned on the cards. On the same tokens, set generation is both more accurate and faster than autoregressive generation. Rigging and secondary motion. Automatic rigging predicts skeleton and skinning weights for given mesh [11, 26, 51, 52, 55, 75]. UniRig [82] also predicts spring bones and their physical attributes on VRoid characters [39], and DRiVE [54] generates skeletons that include hair and skirt bones for anime characters represented as 3D Gaussians. Both rig an existing asset. We generate the spring-bone chains together with the hair they drive, conditioned on the generated cards, and simulate them with the spring-bone update of the VRM specification [62, 63]. 3. Method We propose HairDeck, which generates the cards of hairstyle and the spring-bone chains to animate them  (Fig. 2)  . Each card is encoded into one continuous token (Sec. 3.1), and set diffusion transformer (set DiT) generates all card tokens together, conditioned on single image (Sec. 3.3) or on point cloud (Sec. 3.2), the input of CHARMs benchmark. The card VAE decodes each token back into control points, from which we build the mesh. second set DiT, the chain DiT, generates the spring-bone chains conditioned on the card tokens, and fixed geometric skinning attaches the cards to them (Sec. 3.4). 3.1. Hair cards as tokens Cards. Like CHARM [15], we describe hair card by polyline of control points (pi, wi, hi), each with position pi R3, width wi and thickness hi. We add two attributes that this description leaves out: the cross-section type s, rhombic or triangular, instead of one rhombic crosssection for all cards, and the root normal d1, the width direction of the card at its root, read from the artist mesh instead of being estimated from the first three control points. We widen the appearance of the renders with synthetic style augmentation, such as halftone, XDoG [67] line drawings, flat colors and painterly filters (Sec. We simulate the chains with the VRM spring-bone update of UniVRM [62, 63], using the predicted stiffness and the drag and gravity of most VRoid chains. 3.5. Implementation details The card VAE has four encoder and four decoder layers of width 256, the set DiT 12 layers of width 768 (181.3M parameters) and the chain DiT 8 layers of width 384 (30.5M). We train the point-cloud model for 80K steps with batch size 64 and the image model for 100K steps with batch size 48, both with AdamW [29] at learning rate 104; the image model starts from the point-cloud model. We sample with 50 Euler steps and guidance scale of 2; Sec. lists the remaining settings. 4. Experiments 4.1. Setup Data. We use the dataset of CHARM [15], built from VRoid characters [39]: we take 36,440 of its training hairstyles and test on its 100 test hairstyles, with the point clouds CHARM released. For single images, we render the front views of the 76 test characters whose complete models are available, and we collect 40 in-the-wild images, anime illustrations sampled at random and stratified by hairstyle. 6 Metrics. On point clouds we follow CHARMs protocol: it compares the generated cards with its ground truth, rebuilt from its card templates, by Chamfer distance (CD), earth movers distance (EMD), Hausdorff distance (HD) and voxel IoU. As the templates estimate card orientations, we also evaluate against the original artist meshes. Our orientation metric matches every generated card to the artist card closest in CD and averages the angle between their width directions over 32 positions along the card. Root precision and recall are the shares of generated and groundtruth cards whose root position lies within 2% of the character height of root position in the other set. For single images, we align every output to the ground truth (Sec. D) and report the aligned CD and IoU on surface samples. The failure rate is the share of results that have fewer than 25% of the ground-truth cards (16 cards for in-the-wild images) or leave the scalp bare (hair covers less than 80% of the top or the back of the head); for the image-to-3D generators, whose output is one fused surface without cards, only the scalp criterion applies. Hair colors and head placements are blended for display. 4.6. Applications Interpolation. The Dora encoder computes the condition tokens of point cloud at query points that farthest point sampling picks from it, so the tokens of two point clouds have no correspondence. To interpolate between two conditions, we match the tokens of the second to those of the first by Hungarian matching on the positions of their query points and blend the matched tokens linearly  (Fig. 9)  . Rigging existing hairstyles. The chain DiT reads only card tokens, so it can also rig card hairstyles that an artist modeled without spring bones; its evaluation on the artists cards in Sec. 4.5 measures this use. 5. Limitations and Conclusion Limitations. HairDeck learns from stylized VRoid hairstyles, so very short hair and the alpha-textured cards of realistic hair lie outside its training data. It generates the geometry and UV coordinates of the cards but no textures. Some VRoid characters model bows and hats with hair cards, so HairDeck generates them as cards when the input shows them; filtering such cards from the training data would avoid this. The chain DiT follows the chain layouts common among VRoid characters and generates fewer chains for unusual ones, such as many chains radiating from the crown. Figure 23 shows failure cases. Conclusion. HairDeck generates the stylized hair cards of character and the spring-bone chains that animate them from single image. Treating hairstyle as an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, with one token per card and all tokens generated together, makes generation more accurate and faster than autoregressive decoding, and the same recipe generates the chains. Assets built from other artist-defined primitives, such as garments sewn from panels or drawings made of strokes, can be generated in the same way.
